title: Part 2, Chapter 7
paragraphs: About what passed between Don Quixote and his squire, along with other very notable incidents

The instant the housekeeper saw Sancho Panza shut himself in with her master, she guessed what they were up to; and suspecting that the upshot of the consultation would be a decision to make a third sally, she grabbed her cloak and, distraught with worry, ran to find the bachelor Sansón Carrasco — figuring that, being a well-spoken man and a recent friend of her master's, he might be able to talk him out of any such mad notion. She found him pacing the patio of his house, and the moment she saw him, sweating and flustered, she threw herself at his feet.
Carrasco, seeing how distressed and overcome she was, said to her, "What is this, mistress housekeeper? What's happened? You look heartbroken."
"Nothing, Señor Sansón," she said, "only that my master is breaking out — plainly breaking out."
"Whereabouts is he breaking out, señora?" asked Sansón. "Has some part of his body burst?"

"He's only breaking out at the door of his madness," she replied. "I mean, dear señor bachelor, that he's going to break out again — and this will be the third time — to hunt all over the world for what he calls ventures, though I can't see why he gives them that name. The first time he was brought back to us slung across the back of a donkey, beaten black and blue; the second he came in an ox-cart, locked up in a cage, in which he had persuaded himself he was enchanted, and the poor creature was in such a state that the mother who bore him wouldn't have known him — lean, yellow, with his eyes sunk deep in the sockets of his skull; so that to bring him round again, even a little, cost me more than six hundred eggs, as God knows, and all the world, and my hens too, who won't let me tell a lie."

"That I can well believe," replied the bachelor, "for they are so good and so fat, and so well-bred, that they wouldn't say one thing for another, even if they had to burst for it. So in short, mistress housekeeper, that's all — there's nothing the matter except what it is feared Don Quixote may do?"
"No, señor," she said.

"Well then," the bachelor returned, "don't be upset, but go home in peace; get me something hot ready for breakfast, and while you're on your way say the prayer of Santa Apollonia — if you know it; for I'll come along shortly and you'll see miracles."
"Woe is me," cried the housekeeper, "is it the prayer of Santa Apollonia you'd have me say? That would do if my master had toothache; but what he's got is in the brains."

"I know what I'm saying, mistress housekeeper. Go, and don't set yourself to argue with me, for you know I'm a bachelor of Salamanca, and one can't be more of a bachelor than that," replied Carrasco; and with that the housekeeper went off, and the bachelor went to find the curate to arrange with him what will be told in its proper place.

While Don Quixote and Sancho were shut up together, they had a discussion that the history records with great precision and scrupulous exactness. Sancho said to his master, "Señor, I have educed my wife to let me go with your worship wherever you choose to take me."
"Induced, you should say, Sancho," said Don Quixote, "not educed."

"Once or twice, as I remember," replied Sancho, "I've begged your worship not to mend my words, if so be as you understand what I mean by them; and if you don't understand them, to say 'Sancho,' or 'devil,' 'I don't understand you'; and if I don't make my meaning plain, then you may correct me, for I'm so focile —"
"I don't understand you, Sancho," said Don Quixote at once, "for I don't know what 'I'm so focile' means."
"'So focile' means I'm so much that way," replied Sancho.
"I understand you still less now," said Don Quixote.
"Well, if you can't understand me," said Sancho, "I don't know how to put it; I know no more, God help me."
"Oh, now I've got it," said Don Quixote. "You mean you are so docile, tractable, and gentle that you'll take in what I say to you, and submit to what I teach you."
"I'd bet," said Sancho, "that from the very first you understood me and knew what I meant, but you wanted to throw me off so you could hear me make another couple of dozen blunders."
"Maybe so," replied Don Quixote. "But to come to the point — what does Teresa say?"

"Teresa says," replied Sancho, "that I should make sure with your worship, and 'let papers speak and beards be still,' for 'he who binds does not wrangle,' since one 'take' is better than two 'I'll give you's; and I say a woman's advice is no great thing, and he who won't take it is a fool."
"And so say I," said Don Quixote. "Continue, my friend Sancho; go on — you talk pearls today."

"The fact is," Sancho went on, "that, as your worship knows better than I do, we're all of us liable to death — today we are, tomorrow we are not, the lamb goes as quickly as the sheep, and nobody can promise himself more hours of life in this world than God may be pleased to give him; for death is deaf, and when it comes to knock at our life's door, it's always urgent, and neither prayers, nor struggles, nor sceptres, nor mitres can hold it back — as common talk and report say, and as they tell us from the pulpits every day."
"All that is very true," said Don Quixote, "but I can't make out what you're driving at."

"What I'm driving at," said Sancho, "is that your worship settle some fixed wages on me, to be paid monthly while I'm in your service, and that the same be paid me out of your estate; for I don't care to stand on rewards that either come late, or come ill, or never at all — God help me with my own. In short, I'd like to know what I'm to get, be it much or little; for the hen will lay on one egg, and many littles make a much, and so long as one gains something there's nothing lost. To be sure, if it should happen (what I neither believe nor expect) that your worship were to give me that island you've promised me, I'm not so ungrateful nor so grasping that I wouldn't be willing to have the revenue of such an island valued and deducted from my wages in due promotion."
"Sancho, my friend," replied Don Quixote, "sometimes proportion may be as good as promotion."
"I see," said Sancho. "I'll bet I ought to have said proportion, not promotion; but it doesn't matter, since your worship has understood me."

"And so well understood," Don Quixote returned, "that I've seen into the depths of your thoughts, and know the target you're shooting at with the countless arrows of your proverbs. Look here, Sancho, I'd happily fix your wages if I had ever found a single instance in the histories of the knights-errant to show or hint, by the slightest indication, what their squires used to get monthly or yearly; but I've read all or most of their histories, and I can't remember reading of any knight-errant having assigned fixed wages to his squire. I only know that they all served on reward, and that when they least expected it, if good luck attended their masters, they found themselves rewarded with an island or something equivalent to it, or at the very least left with a title and lordship. If on those terms — with those hopes and added inducements — you, Sancho, choose to come back into my service, well and good. But to suppose that I'm going to disturb or unhinge the ancient usage of knight-errantry is nonsense. So, my Sancho, get yourself back to your house and explain my intentions to your Teresa, and if she's content and you're content to be on reward with me, _bene quidem;_ if not, we remain friends. For if the pigeon-house does not lack food, it will not lack pigeons; and bear in mind, my son, that a good hope is better than a bad holding, and a good grievance better than a bad compensation. I speak this way, Sancho, to show you I can shower down proverbs just as well as you can; and in short, I mean to say, and I do say, that if you don't want to come on reward with me and run the same risks I run, God be with you and make a saint of you. I'll find plenty of squires more obedient and conscientious, and not so thick-headed or talkative as you are."

When Sancho heard his master's firm, resolute words, a cloud came over his sky and the wings of his heart drooped, for he had been sure that his master wouldn't go without him for all the wealth of the world; and as he stood there dumbfounded and gloomy, Sansón Carrasco came in with the housekeeper and the niece, who were eager to hear the arguments he was about to use to dissuade their master from going off in search of adventures. That arch wag Sansón stepped forward and, embracing Don Quixote as before, said in a loud voice, "O flower of knight-errantry! O shining light of arms! O honour and mirror of the Spanish nation! May Almighty God in his infinite power grant that any person or persons who would impede or hinder your third sally may find no way out of the labyrinth of their schemes, nor ever accomplish what they most desire!" Then, turning to the housekeeper, he said, "Mistress housekeeper may as well give over saying the prayer of Santa Apollonia, for I know it is the positive determination of the spheres that Señor Don Quixote shall proceed to carry out his new and lofty designs; and I'd lay a heavy burden on my conscience if I didn't urge and persuade this knight not to keep the strength of his mighty arm and the virtue of his valiant spirit curbed and checked any longer, since by his inactivity he is defrauding the world of the redress of wrongs, of the protection of orphans, of the honour of virgins, of the aid of widows, and of the support of wives, and other matters of this kind belonging, proper, and peculiar to the order of knight-errantry. On, then, my lord Don Quixote, beautiful and brave — let your worship and highness set out today rather than tomorrow; and if anything is needed for the execution of your purpose, here am I, ready in person and in purse to supply the want; and if it were necessary to attend your magnificence as squire, I'd count it the happiest good fortune."

At this, Don Quixote turned to Sancho and said, "Didn't I tell you, Sancho, there'd be squires enough and to spare for me? See who's offering to become one now — no less than the illustrious bachelor Sansón Carrasco, the perpetual joy and delight of the courts of the Salamancan schools, sound in body, discreet, patient under heat or cold, hunger or thirst, with every quality a knight-errant's squire requires! But heaven forbid that, to indulge my own inclination, I should shake or shatter this pillar of letters and vessel of the sciences, or cut down this towering palm of the fair and liberal arts. Let this new Sansón remain in his own country and, by bringing honour to it, bring honour at the same time on the grey heads of his venerable parents; for I'll be content with any squire who comes to hand, since Sancho doesn't deign to come with me."

"I do deign," said Sancho, deeply moved and with tears in his eyes. "It shan't be said of me, master mine," he went on, "'the bread eaten and the company dispersed.' I come of no ungrateful stock, for all the world knows — but particularly my own town — who the Panzas I'm descended from were; and, what's more, I know and have learned, from many kind words and deeds, your worship's wish to show me favour; and if I've been bargaining more or less about my wages, it was only to please my wife, who, when she sets herself to press a point, no hammer drives the hoops of a cask the way she drives you to do what she wants. But after all, a man must be a man and a woman a woman; and as I'm a man anyhow — which I can't deny — I'll be one in my own house too, let who will take it amiss. So there's nothing more to do but for your worship to make your will with its codicil in such a way that it can't be provoked, and let us set out at once, to save Señor Sansón's soul from suffering, as he says his conscience obliges him to persuade your worship to sally out into the world a third time. So I offer again to serve your worship faithfully and loyally, as well as and better than all the squires who served knights-errant in times past or present."

The bachelor was amazed when he heard Sancho's phrasing and style of talk, for though he had read the first part of his master's history he had never imagined Sancho could be as droll as he was described there; but now, hearing him talk of a "will and codicil that could not be provoked" instead of "will and codicil that could not be revoked," he believed everything he had read of him, and set him down as one of the greatest simpletons of modern times; and he said to himself that two such lunatics as master and man the world had never seen. In the end, Don Quixote and Sancho embraced one another and made friends, and by the advice and with the approval of the great Carrasco — who was now their oracle — it was arranged that their departure should take place three days later, by which time they could have everything ready for the journey and procure a closed helmet, which Don Quixote said he must by all means take. Sansón offered him one, since he knew a friend who had one and would not refuse to lend it, though it was more dingy with rust and mildew than bright and clean like burnished steel.

The curses both housekeeper and niece poured out on the bachelor were past counting; they tore their hair, they clawed their faces, and in the style of the hired mourners that used to be in fashion, they raised a lamentation over the departure of their master and uncle as if it had been his death. Sansón's intention in persuading him to sally forth once more was to do what the history relates further on — all by the advice of the curate and barber, with whom he had previously discussed the matter. Finally, then, during those three days, Don Quixote and Sancho provided themselves with what they considered necessary, and Sancho having pacified his wife and Don Quixote his niece and housekeeper, at nightfall, unseen by anyone except the bachelor — who thought it right to accompany them half a league out of the village — they set out for El Toboso, Don Quixote on his good Rocinante and Sancho on his old Dapple, his alforjas furnished with provisions and his purse with money Don Quixote had given him to meet emergencies. Sansón embraced him and begged him to let him hear of his good or bad fortunes, so that he might rejoice over the former or condole with him over the latter, as the laws of friendship required. Don Quixote promised he would, and Sansón returned to the village, and the other two took the road for the great city of El Toboso.
